Research record · 14 October 2026

Where is all the new, good software?

Evidence, original counts, limitations and a research design for separating more code from more useful software.

The evidence supports a substantial expansion in attempts and releases, concrete useful improvements, and much less certain growth in broadly adopted quality. AI attribution is strongest in specific documented projects and adoption studies; most platform-wide time series establish growth without establishing its cause.

Research designEvidence registerOriginal computationsInterpretation checksDecisive next study

Research design

Four outcomes must remain separate: projects started, software released, software demonstrably useful to somebody, and improvement in users’ lives. Code volume is only an intermediate input. Downloads, reviews and revenue are useful but incomplete indicators of value.

QuestionBest observationMain threat
Is more software being made?Historical flows of distinct releases and accepted catalog entries.Pre-existing growth, duplicates, policy changes and deleted failures.
Is more of it useful?Absolute counts above several audience/use thresholds at 90, 180 and 365 days.Older products have more time; free niche tools may have small but valuable audiences.
Are existing products improving?Stable product panels: reproducible defects fixed, crashes, task success, performance and adopted features.A release can add features without improving the user experience.
Did AI cause the change?Verified adoption with credible controls; randomized access where feasible.Self-selection, changing model generations, demand shocks and disclosure bias.
Is the gain hidden in private tools?Repeat use, successful transactions, retired workflows and measured task savings.Project creation and forecast savings mistaken for sustained use.

Source coverage: app stores; Steam; Show HN; F-Droid; Obsidian; Minecraft and Elder Scrolls modding; open-source and enterprise research; internal-tool vendors; software investment and startup payment data. The search prioritized administrative records, downloadable datasets, original empirical studies and named maintainer/customer reports. This is a structured evidence review, not a preregistered systematic review or a census of all software.

Prefer matched calendar periods and equal product ages. Inspect both absolute success counts and success fractions. Separate AI-assisted coding from AI features, generated artwork, and marketing language. A non-AI-themed product may have been entirely AI-coded, and an AI-themed product may have been written without coding assistance.

Show HN: independent monthly counts

Queried the HN Search API for every complete UTC month from January 2022 through September 2026 using the show_hn,story tags. All responses reported exhaustiveNbHits=true. These are indexed posts, not deduplicated software products. Moderation, deletion, community growth and index changes remain possible influences.

September 2026 had 69.5% more submissions than September 2025, and 4.48 times September 2022. The February 2026 peak was 6,217, followed by substantially lower months; presenting that peak as the current sustained rate would mislead.

Across the first nine months, totals were 7,425 (2022), 10,415 (2023), 12,916 (2024), 19,742 (2025), and 37,622 (2026): a 90.6% increase in the latest comparison. The multi-year pretrend was already rising.

Show HN: ordinary product categories also grew

Downloaded Cotera’s 68,025-row Parquet dataset and grouped rows with is_ai=false. Source classifications are licensed CC BY 4.0; attribution: Cotera, “Show HN Posts Dataset, Categorized by Subject,” updated August 28, 2026. These are title/blurb-derived subject classifications. They neither establish nor exclude AI use during development. August is incomplete; only complete quarters appear here.

QuarterNon-AI-themed postsDistinct authors in that subsetGames / graphics postsSystem / desktop posts
Q1 20253,7473,01730868
Q1 20268,9697,111621198
Q2 20254,3143,49432289
Q2 20265,4974,507409158

Q1 non-AI-themed volume rose 139.4%; Q2 rose 27.4%. Thus the surge is not confined to products marketed as AI tools, but the magnitude changes substantially with the observation period. Scores do not provide an independent quality test: authors compete for finite attention and recent submissions have shorter score-accumulation windows.

Pooling the first half of each year, non-AI-themed submissions rose from 8,061 to 14,466 (+79.5%). Distinct authors in that subset rose from 6,088 to 10,995. The author count is deduplicated across the full half-year and must not be obtained by summing quarterly counts.

Modrinth: admitted mods with explicit AI-code disclosure

Six API queries filter project_type:mod, listing-creation timestamps, disclosure_types:ai_content_code, and (for one query) downloads>=1000. Separate facet arrays are AND conditions. Exact URLs, timestamps, responses and a reproduction script are embedded in the downloads above.

Current surviving listings at October 14Count
All mods77,185
All mods disclosing AI-generated code3,294
Created January–September 202514,296
Created January–September 202630,669
2026 cohort with AI-code disclosure2,560
Disclosed-code 2026 cohort with ≥1,000 downloads868

The two release-window listing totals differ by 114.5%. They are not equal-age adoption cohorts: the 2025 listings have had longer to acquire downloads, leave the platform or be removed. Platform growth and migration are additional confounds. Code disclosure began during 2026 and can describe a later update, so the 8.35% disclosure share is not an estimate of all AI-authored mods or of authorship at original release.

Examples in the disclosed-code cohort include Cobblemon Catch Rate Display (3,116,652 downloads; listing created February 3, 2026), a live capture-probability display, and ATMOSPHERICS, a biome-atmosphere control tool. The existence of heavily downloaded disclosed-code mods is stronger evidence of adopted software than submission totals. It still does not identify the counterfactual contribution of AI or unique users.

F-Droid: union of current and archived app catalogs

Downloaded the official main index and archive index, extracted their JSON, deduplicated by package ID and retained the earliest added timestamp. Main catalog: 4,667 apps; archive: 5,183; union: 6,935. All 2,915 shared IDs had identical added timestamps. The indexes were obtained over HTTPS; this counting exercise did not independently validate JAR signatures.

YearFirst admissions in January–September

2026 admissions were 2.99 times 2025. This is a stronger measure of available software than repository starts, but it remains a catalog-admission measure. Apps can predate admission, and infrastructure or queue-clearing changes can accelerate listing without accelerating creation. The archive union reduces, but cannot eliminate, historical survivor bias.

A deterministic random spot-check (seed 8322) of 12 GitHub-hosted apps admitted June–September 2026 found ten source repositories created in 2026, one in October 2025 and one in November 2021. All were non-forks at the time of inspection. This weakens a pure old-project-relisting explanation in that small subset; it does not establish representative authorship, retention, safety or quality.

Reproduction logic
# HN: monthly UTC intervals; use count, not paginated hit length.
params = {
    "tags": "show_hn,story",
    "hitsPerPage": 0,
    "numericFilters": f"created_at_i>={start},created_at_i<{end}"
}
# GET https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search with encoded params
# Record nbHits and exhaustiveNbHits. Queries are in embedded JSON.

# Cotera: aggregate existing classifications, not an AI-authorship detector.
SELECT posted_quarter, count(*) AS non_ai_themed
FROM read_parquet('show-hn-subjects.parquet')
WHERE NOT is_ai AND posted_quarter IN
  ('2025-Q1','2026-Q1','2025-Q2','2026-Q2')
GROUP BY posted_quarter;

# F-Droid: read index-v1.json inside each official index-v1.jar.
by_id = {}
for app in main_index["apps"] + archive_index["apps"]:
    key = app["packageName"]
    if key not in by_id or app["added"] < by_id[key]["added"]:
        by_id[key] = app
# added is Unix milliseconds; group in UTC. Exclude partial October.

Interpretation checks that changed the answer

  1. A falling success rate does not mean fewer successes. If releases triple and the successful share halves, successful products still increase by 50%. Both absolute counts and shares are necessary. Similarly, a constant share of engineering effort devoted to new features need not imply constant new-feature output.
  2. Flat engagement is not flat welfare. Replacing an inferior app, solving a task faster, removing advertising, working offline or improving privacy can benefit users without creating more downloads or screen time. Conversely, more installs do not prove benefit.
  3. Growth and causation are distinct. A clear software supply response across multiple communities is evidence against “nothing is being released.” Its attribution to AI requires a separate argument. Demand for AI products, lower hosting costs, platform growth and new distribution tools can also affect entry.
  4. Completion gains can be substantial despite attenuation. A 30% increase in releases is economically meaningful. The fact that commits rise much faster does not turn the release improvement into zero.
  5. Review congestion is documented in specific workflows. It does not explain all solo projects or establish what proportion of missing consumer value is due to organizational process. Additional marginal products may also have little demand.
  6. Store and disclosure policies matter. Obsidian cleared a review backlog. Modrinth changed acceptance and disclosure rules. Steam AI-content disclosures principally concern player-consumed material, not coding efficiency. None supplies a clean stable treatment indicator.
  7. Current frontier models are largely outside the research windows. Opus 4.5 launched November 24, 2025; Opus 5 July 24, 2026; Astra September 3, 2026. As of October 14, the latter two have only about 12 and 6 weeks of post-release history. Research through March/April cannot evaluate them, although it remains relevant to the earlier agent period.
  8. Preserve negative evidence without exaggerating it. No industry-wide measure found here establishes a comparable explosion in maintained, broadly adopted, high-quality products. That is an unresolved empirical claim, not proof that hidden benefits account for everything or that all extra output is worthless.

Other tempting measures were deliberately kept secondary: cumulative vendor project totals; package-upload counts that conflate distribution files with package versions; raw GitHub activity; unadjusted revenue shares of young versus old apps; and forecasts of hours saved. Some current all-app growth estimates from the same data vendor conflict, so the main answer avoids presenting a single precise 2026 market-wide growth rate.

The most informative next study

Build an absolute useful-output series. Draw release cohorts from several stable ecosystems, deduplicate ports and re-announcements, and follow each at 90, 180 and 365 days. Report how many remain functional, receive maintenance, have repeat external users, and clear several modest and substantial audience thresholds. Keep small privately useful software in a separate stratum with actual workflow-use logs.

ComponentConcrete designWhat it resolves
Public release panelF-Droid, Steam, Chrome extensions, Obsidian, established-game mods; maintain historical snapshots including removals.Whether more completed, maintained ordinary software exists.
Independent usefulness auditRandom stratified sample; reviewers blinded to coding method test a stated user task, defects and task completion time.Whether extra products work and improve on available alternatives.
Repeated-use outcomes90/180-day retained users, repeat transactions, or verified continued private use; absolute counts at multiple thresholds.Whether a growing useful long tail is hidden by falling success percentages.
Incumbent product panelTrack crash rates, reproducible issue fixes, adopted features and task performance in a stable set of products.Benefits that do not create new application identities.
Coding provenanceConsenting developers’ tool telemetry and dated disclosures, independent of AI features and assets.Whether AI assistance predicts the measured changes.
Causal experimentRandomize substantial AI access among builders with real planned projects; add a second treatment for review/release support.Whether cheaper coding raises completed useful output, and whether downstream help unlocks further gains.

The most valuable partner data would link AI use to a work item, a deployment and an actual user outcome. Hosting platforms could supply de-identified creation cohorts with previews, bots and the builder’s own visits excluded. Without that linkage, many precise-looking charts still measure activity rather than useful output.
